summary.text: For \(n=473165\), the number \(M=5292270077783=a(n)+4\) lies strictly between the two proposed endpoints. It is odd and greater than one, and a covering calculation modulo \(48\) using \(\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}\) shows that for every exponent \(j>0\), one of these nontrivial divisors divides \(M2^j+1\), making every such number composite and hence making \(M\) a Sierpiński number.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810n.
\]
Recall that a Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(K>1\) such that
\[
K2^j+1
\]
is composite for every positive integer \(j\).

We disprove the conjecture by taking
\[
n=473{,}165
\]
and exhibiting a third Sierpiński number strictly between \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\).

First compute
\[
11{,}184{,}810\cdot473{,}165=5{,}292{,}260{,}623{,}650,
\]
so
\[
a(473{,}165)
 =9{,}454{,}129+5{,}292{,}260{,}623{,}650
 =5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}779.
\]
Define
\[
M=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783=a(473{,}165)+4.
\]
We will prove that \(M\) is a Sierpiński number. Since
\[
a(473{,}165)<M=a(473{,}165)+4<a(473{,}165)+28,
\]
this will show that the two proposed endpoints are not consecutive Sierpiński numbers.

The proof that \(M\) is Sierpiński uses the covering set
\[
\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}.
\]
We first record the residues of \(M\) modulo these numbers. Direct integer division gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p&\lfloor M/p\rfloor&M\bmod p\\ \hline
3&1{,}764{,}090{,}025{,}927&2\\
5&1{,}058{,}454{,}015{,}556&3\\
7&756{,}038{,}582{,}540&3\\
17&311{,}310{,}004{,}575&8\\
97&54{,}559{,}485{,}337&94\\
257&20{,}592{,}490{,}575&8\\
673&7{,}863{,}699{,}966&665.
\end{array}
\]
Thus, respectively,
\[
M\equiv2,3,3,8,94,8,665
 \pmod{3,5,7,17,97,257,673}.
\]

We also need the following periods of powers of \(2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p&\text{a period for powers of }2\pmod p\\ \hline
3&2\\
5&4\\
7&3\\
17&8\\
257&16\\
97&48\\
673&48.
\end{array}
\]
In other words, \(2^d\equiv1\pmod p\) for each displayed pair \((p,d)\). The first four claims follow immediately from
\[
2^2=4\equiv1\pmod3,
\quad 2^4=16\equiv1\pmod5,
\quad 2^3=8\equiv1\pmod7,
\quad 2^8=256\equiv1\pmod{17}.
\]
For \(257\),
\[
2^{16}=65{,}536=255\cdot257+1.
\]
For \(97\), repeated squaring gives
\[
2^8=256\equiv62,
\qquad
2^{16}\equiv62^2=3844\equiv61,
\qquad
2^{32}\equiv61^2=3721\equiv35
\pmod{97},
\]
and hence
\[
2^{48}=2^{32}2^{16}\equiv35\cdot61=2135=22\cdot97+1\equiv1\pmod{97}.
\]
For \(673\), we have
\[
2^{16}=65{,}536=97\cdot673+255,
\]
so
\[
2^{16}\equiv255,
\qquad
2^{32}\equiv255^2=65{,}025\equiv417
\pmod{673}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{48}=2^{32}2^{16}\equiv417\cdot255
 =106{,}335=158\cdot673+1
 \equiv1\pmod{673}.
\]
All the listed periods therefore divide \(48\).

Now let \(j\) be any positive integer and write
\[
j=48q+r,\qquad 0\le r<48.
\]
For each modulus in the covering set, the period just established divides \(48\). Therefore
\[
2^j=2^{48q+r}\equiv2^r\pmod p.
\]
We split into all possible values of the residue \(r\).

1. Suppose \(r\) is even. Since \(j\) is then even and \(2^2\equiv1\pmod3\), we have \(2^j\equiv1\pmod3\). As \(M\equiv2\pmod3\),
\[
M2^j+1\equiv2\cdot1+1=3\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Thus \(3\mid M2^j+1\). This covers the 24 residues
\[
0,2,4,\ldots,46.
\]

2. Among the odd residues, suppose \(r\equiv3\pmod4\). Then \(2^j\equiv2^3=8\equiv3\pmod5\). Because \(M\equiv3\pmod5\),
\[
M2^j+1\equiv3\cdot3+1=10\equiv0\pmod5.
\]
Thus \(5\mid M2^j+1\). This covers
\[
3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35,39,43,47.
\]

It remains only to consider the odd residues congruent to \(1\pmod4\), namely
\[
1,5,9,13,17,21,25,29,33,37,41,45.
\]
They split into the following five cases.

3. If
\[
r\in\{1,13,25,37\},
\]
then \(r\equiv1\pmod3\). Since powers of \(2\) have period \(3\) modulo \(7\),
\[
2^j\equiv2^r\equiv2\pmod7.
\]
Using \(M\equiv3\pmod7\), we obtain
\[
M2^j+1\equiv3\cdot2+1=7\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
Hence \(7\mid M2^j+1\).

4. If
\[
r\in\{9,17,33,41\},
\]
then \(r\equiv1\pmod8\). Powers of \(2\) have period \(8\) modulo \(17\), so
\[
2^j\equiv2\pmod{17}.
\]
As \(M\equiv8\pmod{17}\),
\[
M2^j+1\equiv8\cdot2+1=17\equiv0\pmod{17}.
\]
Thus \(17\mid M2^j+1\).

5. If
\[
r\in\{5,21\},
\]
then \(r\equiv5\pmod{16}\). Since powers of \(2\) have period \(16\) modulo \(257\),
\[
2^j\equiv2^5=32\pmod{257}.
\]
Together with \(M\equiv8\pmod{257}\), this gives
\[
M2^j+1\equiv8\cdot32+1=257\equiv0\pmod{257}.
\]
Hence \(257\mid M2^j+1\).

6. Suppose \(r=29\). We calculate \(2^{29}\) modulo \(97\). From the computations above,
\[
2^{16}\equiv61,
\qquad
2^8\equiv62
\pmod{97}.
\]
Now
\[
61\cdot62=3782\equiv96\equiv-1\pmod{97}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2^{29}=2^{16}2^8 2^4 2
 \equiv(-1)\cdot16\cdot2
 =-32\equiv65\pmod{97}.
\]
Since \(M\equiv94\pmod{97}\),
\[
M2^j+1\equiv94\cdot65+1=6111=63\cdot97\equiv0\pmod{97}.
\]
Thus \(97\mid M2^j+1\).

7. Finally, suppose \(r=45\). We calculate \(2^{45}\) modulo \(673\). We already know
\[
2^{32}\equiv417\pmod{673}.
\]
Successively multiplying by \(2^8=256\), \(2^4=16\), and \(2\), we obtain
\[
417\cdot256=106{,}752\equiv418\pmod{673},
\]
\[
418\cdot16=6688\equiv631\pmod{673},
\]
and
\[
631\cdot2=1262\equiv589\pmod{673}.
\]
Thus
\[
2^{45}=2^{32}2^8 2^4 2\equiv589\pmod{673}.
\]
As \(M\equiv665\pmod{673}\),
\[
M2^j+1\equiv665\cdot589+1=391{,}686=582\cdot673\equiv0\pmod{673}.
\]
Hence \(673\mid M2^j+1\).

The cases above cover every residue \(r\in\{0,1,\ldots,47\}\). Consequently, for every positive integer \(j\), the number \(M2^j+1\) is divisible by at least one of
\[
3,5,7,17,97,257,673.
\]
Every one of these divisors is greater than \(1\). Moreover, each is at most \(673\), while
\[
M2^j+1>M>673.
\]
Thus the displayed divisor is always a proper nontrivial divisor of \(M2^j+1\). It follows that \(M2^j+1\) is composite for every positive \(j\).

Finally, \(M=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783\) is odd and is greater than \(1\). Together with the preceding covering argument, this proves that \(M\) is a Sierpiński number.

We have therefore found, at \(n=473{,}165\), the Sierpiński number
\[
M=a(473{,}165)+4
\]
strictly between
\[
a(473{,}165)
\quad\text{and}\quad
a(473{,}165)+28.
\]
Hence these two endpoints cannot be consecutive Sierpiński numbers. Therefore the assertion that \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\) are consecutive Sierpiński numbers for every \(n\ge0\) is false.
